**Given $$\mathbf{f(x_k+\alpha t)\approx f(x_k)+\alpha p^T \nabla f(x_k)}$$, the steepest decent direction is $$\mathbf{-\bigtriangledown f_x}$$** Proof: Let p be a unit vector, hence the unit direction p of most rapid decrease is the solution to the problem $$\min\limits_{p}\:\alpha p^T \nabla f(x_k)\:s.t.\:\|p\|=1$$ Since $$\alpha p^T \nabla f(x_k)=\|p\|\|\nabla f(x_k)\|cos(\theta)=\|\nabla f(x_k)\|cos(\theta)$$ the minimizer is attended when $$cos(\theta)=-1$$. Thus the direction of the steepest decent is the exact opposite of the direction of $$\nabla f(x_k)$$, or $$p=-\frac{\nabla f(x_k)}{\|\nabla f(x_k)\|}$$ **Newton direction** $$f(x_k+p)\approx f_k+p^T \nabla f_k+p^T \nabla^2 f_k p \stackrel{\mbox{def}}{=}m_k(p)$$ Assuming for the moment that $$\nabla^2 f_k$$ is [positive definite](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Positive-definite_matrix), we obtain the Newton direction by finding the vector p that minimizes $$m_k(p)$$ or by setting$$\frac{d(m_k(p))}{dp}=0$$. Let's assume $$\nabla f=\nabla f_k$$ to simplify the derivation. $$\frac{d(m_k(p))}{dp}=\frac{d}{dp}(p^T\nabla f)+\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{dp}(p^T\nabla^2 f p)$$ Note that $$\frac{\partial}{\partial p_i}(p^T \nabla f)=\frac{\partial}{\partial p_i} (\sum\limits_{i} p_i \nabla f_i)={\nabla f}^T$$ and $$\frac{\partial}{\partial p_i}(p^T\nabla^2 f p)=\frac{\partial}{\partial p_i}(\sum\limits_{j}\sum\limits_{k}p_k\nabla^2 f_{kj} p_j)$$ $$=\sum\limits_{j}\nabla^2 f_{ij} p_j+\sum\limits_{k}\nabla^2 f_{ki} p_k$$ $$=p^T{\nabla^2 f}^T+p^T\nabla^2 f$$ $$=2p^T\nabla^2 f$$ ($$\nabla^2 f$$ is symmetric) thus $$\frac{d(m_k(p))}{dp}={\nabla f}^T+p^T\nabla^2 f=\vec{0}^T$$ $$\Rightarrow{\nabla f}+{\nabla^2 f}^T p=\vec{0} $$ $$\Rightarrow{\nabla f}+{\nabla^2 f} p=\vec{0} $$ ($$\nabla^2 f$$ is symmetric) $$\Rightarrow p=-(\nabla^2 f)^{-1}\nabla f$$
